note: Attacker-controlled 8-byte input is interpreted as an H3Index (64-bit) plus an int vertexNum. The index's mode bits and reserved bits are fully attacker-controlled.
The raw attacker-controlled index is passed directly to vertexToLatLng without validating that its mode is H3_VERTEX_MODE.

The reserved bits (bits 3-7) of the attacker-controlled index are extracted as the vertex number. Since the mode was not checked, these bits can be any value 0-31, including values >= 6 which are invalid for hexagon vertices.

code: H3Index owner = vertex; H3_SET_MODE(owner, H3_CELL_MODE); H3_SET_RESERVED_BITS(owner, 0);
note: The mode is forcibly set to H3_CELL_MODE and reserved bits cleared, but the vertexNum extracted in step 3 is retained and used later.
The owner cell is converted to FaceIJK coordinates. If the owner is a valid cell, this succeeds; the attacker can craft an index that is a valid cell in H3_CELL_MODE.

The unvalidated vertexNum (0-31) is passed to _faceIjkToCellBoundary. For a hexagon, valid vertex numbers are 0-5; values >= 6 cause out-of-bounds access into the vertex direction tables, reading uninitialized memory.

The function uses vertexNum to index into static direction tables (e.g., directionToVertexNumHex). An out-of-range vertexNum (>= 6) reads beyond the table bounds, producing an uninitialized or garbage direction value that propagates into the CellBoundary output.
The uninitialized/garbage boundary vertex is copied into the output LatLng structure, which is the use-of-uninitialized-value detected by MemorySanitizer.
